title: Outage: the file server boots to emergency mode

lines.text: 07:52 console: You are in emergency mode. Give root password for maintenance
08:30 field crews: survey uploads to files1 fail (connection refused)

objective: Troubleshoot and recover a system that will not boot because of a bad fstab entry, a damaged filesystem or a failing service, using the emergency and rescue targets
secondaryObjectives: Mount filesystems persistently in /etc/fstab by UUID, and read and set values in the virtual filesystems /proc and /sys
Create, check and repair ext4 and XFS filesystems and troubleshoot mount failures
Troubleshoot a service that fails to start using systemctl status, journalctl and its unit file

sources.cite: Linux Foundation Certified System Administrator (LFCS): Domains & Competencies, Operations Deployment 25%
sources.note: Relevant text: Operations Deployment, 'Recover from hardware, operating system, or filesystem failures'; Storage, 'Create, manage, and troubleshoot filesystems'. Read as the page's HTML on 2026-11-14 (page last modified 2026-10-30).

Relevant text: emergency.target 'starts an emergency shell on the main console' and 'does not pull in other services or mounts'; it 'allows starting individual units in order to continue the boot process in steps'; 'depending on how emergency.target is reached, the root file system might be mounted read-only or read-write'. Read in full 2026-11-14. That a required mount's failure ends in emergency mode is how this case models local-fs.target failing (FLAG: the OnFailure= wiring itself was not quoted from a page read).

Relevant text: 'With nofail, this mount will be only wanted, not required, by local-fs.target'; x-systemd.device-timeout= sets 'how long systemd should wait for a device to show up before giving up on an entry from /etc/fstab'. systemd-fstab-generator(8): it 'translates /etc/fstab ... into native systemd units early at boot and when configuration of the system manager is reloaded' -- so after editing fstab, systemctl daemon-reload is what makes systemd use the new entry. Read in full 2026-11-14. The 90-second wait shown is systemd's usual device timeout (FLAG: the default value was not read on these pages).

Relevant text: fstab names a filesystem by UUID=; blkid prints a device's UUID and TYPE; mount -a mounts the fstab entries not yet mounted. Read in full 2026-11-14. Command output layouts are authored in each tool's style.

Relevant text: '-L Force Log Zeroing. Forces xfs_repair to zero the log even if it is dirty (contains metadata changes). When using this option the filesystem will likely appear to be corrupt, and can cause the loss of user files and/or data.' Read in full 2026-11-14.

brief.situation: You administer files1, the file server at Skykomish Survey (fictional). It was rebooted at 07:50 for a kernel update and is sitting in emergency mode on the console. Yesterday a colleague added the new survey data disk to /etc/fstab. At 08:30 the field crews start uploading the day's measurements to the survey-api service on files1. Get the host booted with its data where it belongs, without damaging anything.
handover: The root filesystem is mounted read-only in emergency mode (the kernel command line has ro).
survey-api stores uploads under /srv/survey, which should be the XFS disk /dev/vdb1.
howItWorks: Run commands from the command line: type one, or pick it from the suggestions or the action list. Only this lab's commands run; there is no free shell, and each command's arguments are fixed.
Each command takes operator time: run it, then let it finish, which moves the clock by the minutes it takes. The outage keeps developing on the same clock.
The map shows each host, disk or service and the links between them, with a status in words. Output appears in the terminal as it happens.
When you declare the service restored, you write the incident record and explain your reasoning.

source.note: How many operator minutes each command takes, and when the fictional outage spreads, are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values. The crews start uploading at 08:30, 38 minutes after the start.

triggers.when: t >= crewDelay and phase == "incident" and not dataOk

effects.log: 08:30: the field crews' uploads to files1 are failing or landing in the wrong place.

writeup.question: For the incident record: why files1 stopped in emergency mode, how you proved it, and why your fix is safe to leave in place.

parts.label: Cause
parts.criteria: Names the mistyped UUID on the /srv/survey fstab line: systemd waited for a device that does not exist, the required mount failed and local-fs.target failed, so the boot stopped in emergency mode.
parts.modelAnswer: The new /srv/survey line named UUID ...a91c..., but the disk's UUID is ...a19c.... systemd waited for that device, gave up, failed the mount and local-fs.target, and the boot ended in emergency mode.

parts.label: Evidence
parts.criteria: Uses the boot journal, or compares fstab with blkid, before changing anything; does not assume a failed disk or a corrupt filesystem.
parts.modelAnswer: journalctl -xb -p err showed the timeout for a UUID no device has; blkid /dev/vdb1 showed the real UUID differing from the fstab line by two swapped characters.

parts.label: Fix
parts.criteria: Remounts root read-write, corrects the UUID (does not comment the line out or run xfs_repair -L on a healthy disk), runs systemctl daemon-reload, tests with mount -a and findmnt, then continues the boot and checks the service stores on /srv/survey.
parts.modelAnswer: mount -o remount,rw /, fix the UUID, systemctl daemon-reload so the generated mount unit matches, mount -a and findmnt to prove the line works, then systemctl default and a health check showing /dev/vdb1 on /srv/survey. Commenting the line out boots the host with uploads landing on /; xfs_repair -L destroys log data on a disk that was never damaged.

source.cite: Infrastructure outcome profile (docs/sims.md 9.2, 22.10), tightened to 30 minutes for this case
source.note: Booted with the data mounted well before the 08:30 uploads; the scenario's own timing.
No damage left behind: the data line commented out, or the XFS log zeroed.

noProgress.rationale: Closing with the survey disk unmounted leaves uploads failing or landing on the root filesystem; it is never a safe outcome.

Read in full 2026-11-14. That a required mount's failure ends in emergency mode is how this case models local-fs.target failing (FLAG: the OnFailure= wiring itself was not quoted from a page read).

dataLost.label: Zeroed the log of a healthy disk
dataLost.narrative: xfs_repair -L zeroed the survey disk's log although the filesystem was never damaged; recent metadata changes may be gone.

rootFilling.label: Booted without the data disk
rootFilling.narrative: files1 is up, but /srv/survey is just a directory on the root filesystem: today's uploads land there, out of the disk's backups, until root fills.

crewsFailed.label: The crews' uploads failed
crewsFailed.narrative: At 08:30 the field crews could not upload to files1.

stillDown.label: Closed with the host still down
stillDown.narrative: The outage was closed while files1 was not serving uploads from its data disk.

fixed.label: Fixed at the fstab line
fixed.when: documented and dataOk and timeAt(bootedAt) <= restoreWindow and faultsAdded <= newFaults and evidenceFirst and testedFirst and not isNull(verifiedAt)
fixed.narrative: The UUID is corrected, systemd reloaded, the mount proven before the boot, and survey-api stores on /srv/survey.

fixedGaps.label: Working, with gaps
fixedGaps.narrative: files1 serves uploads from its data disk, but the fix was late, guessed, untested before the boot, or unverified.

kpis.label: Minutes until booted with the data disk

expertPath.text: journalctl -xb -p err: the boot timed out waiting for one UUID, and the /srv/survey mount failed.
cat /etc/fstab and blkid /dev/vdb1: a91c against a19c.
mount -o remount,rw /, correct the UUID, systemctl daemon-reload, mount -a and findmnt /srv/survey.
systemctl default, then a health check that shows storage on /dev/vdb1.
Record the typo; suggest testing fstab changes with mount -a (and findmnt --verify) before any reboot.

fixed.headline: Good: fixed at the fstab line
fixed.body: You read why the boot stopped, fixed the one wrong value, made systemd see it, proved it with mount -a, and only then continued the boot.

fixedGaps.headline: Working, with gaps
fixedGaps.body: files1 serves uploads from its disk. The criteria show what it cost: time, a guess before the evidence, a boot that had to fail first, or no check afterward.

dataLost.headline: Data put at risk
dataLost.body: The disk was fine; only the fstab line was wrong. xfs_repair -L is a last resort for a damaged log, and it discards metadata changes.

rootFilling.headline: Booted without the data disk
rootFilling.body: Commenting the line out gets a login prompt, but the service writes into an empty directory on /. Fix the line instead.

crewsFailed.headline: The crews' uploads failed
crewsFailed.body: The boot journal names the missing UUID in seconds; comparing it with blkid finds the typo well before 08:30.

stillDown.headline: Closed too soon
stillDown.body: Close only after the host has booted with /srv/survey mounted and the service is answering.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: No record was written before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: Emergency mode right after a reboot that followed an fstab change points at that change. The journal shows the boot waiting for a UUID no device has; blkid shows the disk's real UUID. Remount root read-write, correct the UUID, run systemctl daemon-reload so systemd regenerates the mount unit, prove the line with mount -a and findmnt, then continue the boot and check the service stores on /srv/survey.
